messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Musician
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 45

He still plays the piano, but only in the dark. That is the first thing he tells me, settling into the armchair with the careful stiffness of a man who has learned to measure every movement. His name is Dinh, and at fifty, his hands—those elegant, calloused instruments of a lifetime—now tremble when he reaches for his coffee cup.

The stalking began three years ago, though he didn't name it that at first. He had just finalized his divorce, a quiet dissolution of a twenty-year marriage that had long since become a room with no music. He moved into a small apartment above a dry cleaner in a working-class neighborhood. The building had a fire escape outside his bedroom window, which he found charming until he realized it was also a stairway for anyone who wanted to climb.

It started with small things. A note slipped under his door, folded into the shape of a bird. "I heard you play Chopin last night. You were sad." He dismissed it as a fan—he had a modest following from his years with the city orchestra, and occasional admirers were not unusual. Then the notes became more frequent, sometimes three in a single day. They were always written in the same looping cursive, always on unlined paper torn from a sketchbook.

He began to notice a woman. She was always there, it seemed. At the corner market when he bought his morning tea. Seated alone at the back of the café where he liked to read scores. Once, he looked up from his piano during a rehearsal and saw her face pressed against the glass of the practice room door, her breath fogging the pane.

His response was not fear, at first, but a kind of weary confusion. He tried to be reasonable. He spoke to her once, gently, asking her to stop. She smiled, her eyes too wide, and said, "But how else will I hear your music?"

He changed his route to the rehearsal hall. He stopped going to the café. He drew his blinds, even during the day. But the notes kept coming. They appeared under his windshield wiper, taped to his mailbox, slipped through the gap in his doorframe. The words grew darker. "Your ex-wife doesn't understand you. I do. I see your loneliness. I can take it away."

The night it broke him, he was coming home from a late gig. He saw her standing on the fire escape, her face level with his bedroom window, her hands pressed flat against the glass like a child at a candy shop. She was mouthing words he could not hear. He stood frozen in the alley below, his guitar case still in his hand, and he did not go inside. He slept in his car that night. He has not slept in that bedroom since.

He moved twice in the following year. He changed his phone number three times. He stopped performing in public venues. Now, he teaches piano from his current apartment—a sterile, fourth-floor walk-up with no fire escape and a deadbolt he checks seven times before bed. He tells me this without irony, counting on his fingers. "I check it seven times. Not six. Not eight. Seven."

He cannot play in front of anyone anymore. His students, he says, are children who do not yet know how to judge. But when a parent sits in the corner to watch, his fingers lock. He sees a face in the window, even when there is no window. He hears footsteps in the hallway at night, even when the building is silent. He has lost thirty pounds. His divorce papers, he mentions, are still in a box he has not opened.

He looks at me, his eyes tired but clear. "I used to think music was the one thing no one could take from me," he says. "Now I know that's not true." He does not say what he thinks she took. He does not have to.
